strengths: Clear and well-motivated novelty: the paper identifies a genuine gap — no prior ML framework performs temporally-adaptive modeling of high-speed (supersonic) flows — and proposes a sensible two-phase design (neural CFL timestep prediction + timestep-conditioned neural solver).

The discussion of why the classical CFL condition cannot be directly applied to neural solvers (coarsened space-time meshes, subset of field variables, multiphase complexity) is insightful and justifies learning a surrogate timestep predictor.

Creation and release of two new, physically meaningful supersonic flow datasets (coal dust explosion generated with a validated multiphase solver, circular blast) with detailed problem descriptions, solver settings, and public code/datasets supports reproducibility and community value.

Extensive and systematic evaluation: 4 solver backbones (U-Net, CNO, F-FNO, Transolver) x 3 conditioning strategies (Base, Euler, MoE) x 2 datasets, averaged over 3 training runs with standard errors, plus ablations of physically-motivated neural CFL components (gradients, CFL features, max pooling).

Transparent reporting: one-step, unrolled, correlation time, mean flow, and TKE errors are all tabulated in appendices, including cases where the proposed conditioning does not help, and limitations/future work are candidly discussed.
weaknesses: No comparison against a uniform-timestep neural solver baseline, so the central claim that adaptive time-stepping benefits neural solvers (more balanced objectives, better training) is asserted but not empirically demonstrated; the reader cannot tell how much of the performance comes from the adaptive framework versus the backbone.

The proposed conditioning strategies (Euler residuals, MoE) provide only modest and inconsistent gains over the Base conditioning; in many cases (e.g., Transolver Euler mean flow error 6.83 vs Base 4.22 on circular blast; U-Net Base often best) the new components perform equal to or worse than simpler baselines, weakening the significance of these contributions.
No wall-clock time or speedup comparison against the classical HyBurn solver, despite neural acceleration being a core motivation; the practical value of ShockCast is not quantified.

Generalization is weakly tested: evaluation cases are interpolations within the same parameter ranges (shock Mach 1.2-2.1, IPR up to 50), with small test sets (10 and 9 cases); no extrapolation or out-of-distribution experiments.

Some experimental details complicate fair comparison, e.g., MoE models use a reduced latent dimension (except CNO), and CNO variants have markedly fewer FLOPs than other backbones, so architecture rankings conflate compute budgets.

A few presentation issues: the correlation time for one coal dust field is capped at exactly 80.00 without explanation of the evaluation window; dataset/code URLs are placeholders in the abstract; results in Figures 5-6 are difficult to read precisely without the appendix tables.

strengths: The paper addresses an under-explored problem: temporally adaptive modeling of high-speed (supersonic) flows with neural solvers, and correctly identifies that classical CFL-based timestep selection does not transfer to coarsened neural meshes.

The authors release two new datasets (coal dust explosion, circular blast) generated with a validated CFD solver (HyBurn/AMReX) along with code, which supports reproducibility and could benefit the community.

The evaluation grid is broad: four neural solver backbones (U-Net, CNO, F-FNO, Transolver) crossed with three timestep conditioning strategies, run over 3 seeds, with physically meaningful metrics (correlation time, TKE, mean flow error) reported in detail in the appendix.

The physically-motivated design of the neural CFL model (spatial gradients, max-pooling, CFL features) is sensible, and the ablation in Figure 2 shows these components help in the more challenging multiphase setting.
weaknesses: The central claim that adaptive time-stepping benefits neural solvers is never directly validated. There is no uniform-timestep baseline trained/evaluated on the same data, so it is impossible to tell whether the proposed adaptive framework is actually better than simply training with a fixed (or a few fixed) timestep sizes. This is a fundamental missing ablation for the paper's motivation.

The improvements from the proposed conditioning strategies (Euler Residuals, MoE) over the Base conditioning are marginal and inconsistent. In Tables 3-6 and 9-11, the differences are frequently within or barely outside the reported error bars, and the ordering flips across architectures and datasets (e.g., MoE is best for CNO on circular blast but clearly worse for U-Net in mean flow error, Transolver+Euler degrades substantially). The authors themselves can only identify a different best configuration for each metric/dataset, which suggests no reliable advantage of the proposed methods.

No comparison against existing adaptive/continuous-time approaches (e.g., [72] TanE, [73], [74]) or against a classical baseline. As a 'first framework' claim, at least a best-effort adaptation of a prior continuous-time method on the new datasets would be needed to establish that the two-phase design is the right approach.

The evaluation sets are very small (10 and 9 test cases) with only 3 seeds, and the reported standard errors are often large relative to the differences being claimed; statistical support for the headline conclusions is thin.

The neural CFL one-step errors in Figure 2 are surprisingly high (MAE ~0.55 on normalized dt for coal dust explosion), and no analysis is given of how sensitive the downstream rollout is to CFL prediction error, nor whether a much simpler predictor (e.g., a small network regressing on summary statistics of the CFL features) would suffice.

No wall-clock/runtime comparison against the classical solver is provided, so the practical value of the neural acceleration in this setting is not quantified, despite speedup being a core motivation of neural solvers.

The scope is limited to the supersonic regime on two fairly standard synthetic setups (a 2D blast and a shock-dust channel); the 'high-speed flow' framing (including hypersonics) in the introduction oversells what is actually evaluated.

The correlation time metric uses an arbitrary 0.9 correlation threshold with linear interpolation of predictions onto the ground-truth grid, which can mask error accumulation in shock timing; instantaneous field errors in Figures 17-20 grow to 0.1-0.26 relative error by the end of the rollouts, which the aggregate metrics do not fully convey.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: first ML framework (ShockCast) for temporally-adaptive modeling of high-speed (supersonic) flows, addressing a real gap in the neural PDE solver literature which overwhelmingly focuses on incompressible/uniform-timestep settings.

Physically-grounded design: the neural CFL model's input features (spatial gradients, CFL features, max-pooling downsampling) are clearly derived from the classical CFL condition, and the paper is explicit about why the classical CFL condition cannot be applied directly on coarsened meshes with a subset of field variables.

Comprehensive empirical study: four neural solver backbones (U-Net, CNO, F-FNO, Transolver) crossed with three timestep conditioning strategies, three training seeds with error bars, ablations of the neural CFL inputs (Figure 2), and detailed compute/memory reporting (Table 2).

Significant community resources: two new, challenging high-speed flow datasets (multiphase coal dust explosion; circular blast) generated with a validated production CFD code (HyBurn/AMReX), with code and data released; extensive appendices covering data generation, training, metrics, and visualizations.
Honest treatment of limitations, including discussion of the CFL-supervision choice and future policy-based timestep learning in Appendix G, and a broader impacts statement.
weaknesses: Missing the most important baseline: the paper does not compare against a neural solver trained on a temporally uniform mesh (i.e., the standard approach), which would directly validate the central claim that adaptive time-stepping benefits neural solvers through more balanced objectives. Claims about adaptive stepping's advantage (Section 3.1) remain an argument rather than an experimental finding.

No computational speedup or wall-clock comparison against the classical solver (HyBurn), despite acceleration being the primary motivation of the whole neural-solver line of work. Without FLOP/throughput or cost-per-simulation-time comparisons, the practical significance is unquantified.

Empirical gains from the proposed conditioning strategies are modest and inconsistent: Euler/MoE often improve metrics by amounts comparable to or smaller than the reported error bars (e.g., Tables 5, 6, 8), and MoE sometimes degrades performance (e.g., circular blast mean flow in Table 10, correlation time in Table 7). No statistical significance testing is provided to support the qualitative claims in Section 5.4.

Autoregressive stability is a concern: unrolled errors are substantially worse than one-step errors (e.g., gas velocity y-component ~45% relative error and correlation time proportion of only ~19-22% for the coal dust explosion across all models), suggesting the framework degrades badly on some fields, yet this is not analyzed or mitigated.

Scope limitations: only two 2D supersonic problems, small evaluation sets (9-10 cases), narrow Mach number ranges, and a single qualitative Δt trajectory comparison (Figure 3) rather than quantitative unrolled Δt accuracy across all cases. Claims about the hypersonic regime are speculative given no experiments there.

The novelty claim of 'first framework for learning high-speed flows' is positioned against closely related time-adaptive operator learning work ([72] Tante, [73]) without an empirical or head-to-head comparison, only conceptual differentiation.
